children: By Ashitha Shivaprasad

Gold prices rebounded from a more than one-year low on Monday amid a pause in the dollar rally, while investors looked ahead to upcoming US inflation data for further clues on the interest rate trajectory.
Spot gold

climbed 2.4% to $3,617.68 per ounce by 1242 GMT after hitting its lowest level since September 2025 on Friday. Prices declined 9% last week amid pressure from a hawkish US rate outlook and an AI-linked stocks selloff that prompted some investors to liquidate gold to raise cash.
US gold futures
gained 2.9% to $3,618.10 per ounce.
"I would describe today’s rebound in gold as a stabilization following last week’s sharp selloff, with the weaker US dollar providing some support," said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo.
"The longer-term diversification case for gold remains intact, but near-term volatility is likely to remain high."

The dollar drifted near its highest level in 19 months on Monday as traders took a breather from the stock market rout while bets eased on the Federal Reserve aggressively increasing rates in December.
Market participants continue to price in a 25-basis-point Fed hike in December, while expectations of a larger 50-basis-point increase have eased, according to CME's FedWatch Tool.
Higher rates reduce the appeal of non-yielding bullion.
The October Personal Consumption Expenditures index, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, is due on Wednesday.
Spot silver
climbed 2.7% to $42.31 per ounce after hitting its lowest level since September 2025 on Friday. Platinum
gained 1.2% to $1,314.17 per ounce and palladium

"If gold stabilises and the US dollar/rates backdrop turns friendlier, silver has greater room for positioning to rebuild and could rebound more sharply. Until then, its higher beta remains a double-edged sword," Christopher Wong, precious metals strategist at OCBC, said in a note.
"We continue to favour platinum over palladium on a medium-term basis, while recognising that both can stay vulnerable to the current macro and liquidation backdrop," he added.
